An AI agent is a system that can take actions autonomously — not just answer questions, but read files, write code, run commands, and modify your project. Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot are examples. The course teaches you to direct and coordinate them.

faq.q: What's the difference between an agent and a chatbot?
faq.a: A chatbot responds to messages. An agent takes actions — it can read your codebase, write code, run tests, deploy, and iterate. The course teaches you to go from understanding how a single agent works to orchestrating parallel agents coordinating on a shared codebase.

faq.q: What are tokens and context windows?
faq.a: Tokens are the units AI models use to process text — roughly 3/4 of a word. A context window is the total amount of tokens an agent can 'see' at once. Understanding these is foundational to directing agents effectively. Tier 1 covers this in depth.

A context window is the total amount of information an AI agent can process at once — measured in tokens. When you exceed it, the agent loses earlier context. Tier 1 teaches you how to manage context strategically so your agents don't lose track of what they're building.

Agentic refers to AI systems that can act autonomously — reading, writing, and executing code rather than just generating text. An agentic workflow is one where AI agents do the building while you direct and verify. This course teaches multi-agent orchestration — coordinating parallel agents on a shared codebase through task decomposition, git worktrees, and cross-agent verification.

Claude Code is Anthropic's AI coding agent that runs in your terminal. It can read your codebase, write code, run commands, and iterate on feedback. It's the primary tool used throughout the course — you'll learn to run multiple Claude Code instances in parallel via git worktrees with shared context via CLAUDE.md. The multi-agent orchestration patterns transfer to any agent system.

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. MCP servers are plugins that extend what an AI agent can do — connecting it to databases, APIs, file systems, and other tools. Tier 1 teaches you to configure and use them to give your agents superpowers.

You decompose a complex task into independent subtasks, spin up parallel agents in isolated git worktrees on the same codebase, share context between them via CLAUDE.md, verify their outputs with cross-agent verification, resolve conflicts, and merge the results. It's like being a tech lead managing a team — except the team is AI. Tier 3 covers this in depth.

Instead of prompting an agent with vague instructions, you write a precise specification — inputs, outputs, constraints, edge cases. The spec becomes the contract between you and the agent. Tier 2 teaches this as the foundation of reliable agent-directed development.

faq.q: What is the difference between prompting and orchestrating?
faq.a: Prompting is asking a single AI to do one thing. Orchestrating is designing workflows where parallel agents coordinate on a shared codebase — with cross-agent verification, task decomposition, git worktrees for isolation, shared context, conflict resolution, and failure handling. It's the jump from using AI to directing AI at scale.

faq.q: Can agents really build production software?
faq.a: Yes — but only if you know how to direct and coordinate them. Raw agents produce code that compiles but doesn't belong. The course teaches spec-driven development, cross-agent verification, and multi-agent orchestration patterns that turn agent output into production-quality software.

They will — constantly. That's expected. The course teaches verification patterns (Tier 2), cross-agent verification and conflict resolution across parallel agents (Tier 3), and override judgment at the architecture level (Tier 4) so you catch errors before they ship. The skill isn't avoiding mistakes, it's catching them fast.

No. Prompt engineering is about crafting better inputs for a chatbot. This course is about multi-agent orchestration from first principles — coordinating parallel agents on a shared codebase through task decomposition, git worktrees, shared context, and cross-agent verification. Prompt engineering is one small tool in a much larger toolkit.

faq.q: What languages or frameworks do I need to know?
faq.a: Basic JavaScript/TypeScript is the minimum. The course uses Next.js, Supabase, and Vercel, but you don't need prior experience with these — agents help build with them. You need to read code, not write everything from scratch.

faq.q: How is Tier 3 different from Tier 2?
faq.a: Tier 2 teaches you to direct a single agent through specs, constraints, and verification. Tier 3 teaches multi-agent orchestration — coordinating parallel agents on a shared codebase using git worktrees, task decomposition, shared codebase context via CLAUDE.md, cross-agent verification, conflict resolution, and handling failures when agent-built systems break.

Tier 4 is about system-level judgment — architecting systems that agent fleets can build, task decomposition at the architecture level, evaluating AI decisions, knowing when to split/merge/override agent workflows. Your capstone proves you can think at the architecture level, which is the one thing agents can't do for you.
